articles.summary: Martin Soto, a Peruvian man thrown into solitary confinement after organizing a hunger and labor strike inside the notorious for-profit ICE detention facility Delaney Hall , was released from New Jersey’s Elizabeth Detention Center with an ankle monitor Tuesday night . Soto came to the United States in 2024 and was pursuing asylum. He was detained by federal agents in February while buying diapers for his two young children. Though he has no criminal record, he spent eight consecutive months in ICE detention, including several months in solitary confinement—retribution, his wife Gabriela said, for his role as an organizer. Gabriela Soto organized a series of protests outside Delaney Hall in May, as her husband worked to improve conditions inside. On May 22, a group of over 300 detained immigrants, including Martin, announced a two-week hunger and labor strike inside the for-profit detention facility, demanding freedom and due process , as well as a meeting with the governor and an end to coercive pressure to self-deport. The state of New Jersey sued to close Delaney Hall as reports of inedible food, violent guards, and inadequate medical care continued to emerge from the facility.

articles.author: Liz Hoffman
articles.summary: Wall Street’s required reading this week runs 20 pages, carries an “Attorney Advertising” label, and tells financiers exactly how their favorite trade is going to blow up. Law firm Quinn Emanuel’s March memo on data-center debt was making the rounds in recent days, laying out worst-case scenarios for the hundreds of billions of dollars being borrowed and spent to fund the AI buildout. It does the one thing professional-services memos never do: It names names. A Google-backed project in upstate New York is full of holes, the law firm notes: Google’s backstop doesn’t start until construction is complete; deal documents contemplate a “disagreement” about whether it’s been triggered at all; and a six-month delay would let the tenant, AI company Fluidstack, walk away. Meta’s $28 billion Louisiana complex, CoreWeave’s GPU-backed loans, and Oracle’s off-balance sheet lease obligations get a similar legal dissection. “Insolvency cascades” are set off by depreciating GPUs. Collateral food fights and margin calls ensue. Quinn Emanuel is a litigation boutique, so it’s talking its book. But business-development brochures were never such grim reading. — Liz Hoffman
